title: Carmichael's λ and the group structure of (ℤ/4C)^× : choosing C with (ℤ/4C)^× cyclic of small order to make −1 'easy to hit'
connection: For C = 1: (ℤ/4)^× = {±1}; a single factor ≡ 3 mod 4 suffices. For C = p': (ℤ/4p')^× ≅ ℤ/2 × ℤ/(p'−1). −1 is the unique element of order 2 in the cyclic part… the chance a random subset product hits −1 is ≈ 1/φ(4C) per product, but the number of products is 2^ω. Choosing C with φ(4C) small relative to 2^{ω(4Cp+1)}: C prime-power-ish and 4Cp+1 very composite.
why: Optimising the choice of C-family by group structure is a cheap heuristic refinement; could yield a family of C where the win probability is bounded below (e.g. C with 4C | something).
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁶, among winning C ≤ 10⁴, histogram φ(4C)/2^{ω(4Cp+1)}.

title: Poisson–Dirichlet model for the factorisation of 4Cp+1 and subset-product coverage of −1
connection: Large prime factors of a random integer follow the Poisson–Dirichlet(1) law (Billingsley). Combining it with uniform classes of factors in (ℤ/4C)^× gives an exact model probability that no divisor is ≡ −1 (mod 4C).
why: It gives a principled per-level failure probability, which can be aggregated over levels with the correlation structure.
first_step: Simulate PD(1) factorisations with random classes for C ≤ 30; compare P(fail) with empirical per-level failure for 4Cp+1, p < 10⁸.
alt_first_steps: [free_fable-0222] Simulate: for p ≈ 10¹⁸ (no factoring needed — sample Poisson–Dirichlet factorisations), estimate P(fail at (c,d)) for (c,d) ≤ 100; sum.
refs: Billingsley, On the distribution of large prime divisors (1972)

title: Heuristic repair: the expected-count heuristic for the C-form must be corrected by the forced QNR condition — only divisors a with (a/p) = −1 count, halving the expectation; and if a second hidden constraint exists it halves again — is 409's zero count explainable by a cascade of such 'free' constraints?
connection: Each forced symbol halves the expected count; the observed 0 for 409 at expected ≈ 52 (or 26 after QNR) would need ~5–6 independent forced constraints. Alternatively, a single structural obstruction. Determine which by finding the forced-symbol set empirically: for all C-form certificates (over many p), tabulate the joint distribution of (a/q) for small q, a mod 16, etc., and see which symbols are forced (always equal) vs free.
why: Systematic discovery of forced constraints on certificates is a well-defined computation and could reveal the complete 'reciprocity signature' of the C-form, of which (a/p) = −1 is the first element.
first_step: Collect ~10⁵ certificates (p ≤ 10⁵, C ≤ 200); for each candidate symbol s(a, p, C) in a list of ~50 (Jacobi symbols, residues mod small powers of 2, Kronecker symbols (a/2), (−1/a), (p/u)...), compute entropy of its distribution; list zero-entropy ones.

title: Random energy model (Derrida) as null model for certificate counts
connection: REM: 2^N independent energies; ground-state statistics ↔ R(p) as count of ≍ p log p rare independent-ish events with polylog mean.
why: REM predicts Poisson zero probability exp(−mean); calibrating ES's zero probability against REM vs correlated models (GREM) quantifies 'how independent' the events are.
first_step: Fit the empirical distribution of R(p)/M(p) over primes ≤ 10⁸ to Poisson vs negative-binomial vs log-normal; report best-fit dispersion.

title: Large deviations: rate function for lower tail of R(p)
connection: Lower tail P(R(p) ≤ εM) in a random model ↔ Janson inequality for sums of dependent indicators.
why: Janson's inequality gives exp(−μ²/(2Δ)) bounds; computing Δ (pair correlation of certificate events) explicitly for ES yields a falsifiable heuristic and identifies dangerous correlations.
first_step: Compute Δ = Σ_{i~j} P(A_i ∧ A_j) for ES certificate events empirically (pairs of (u,C) sharing a modulus factor) at p ~ 10⁷.

title: Random matrix statistics of the sequence R(p)/M(p)
connection: Fluctuations of arithmetic counts often match RMT (e.g. L-function zeros) ↔ R(p) normalised.
why: If fluctuations are Gaussian with variance ~ (log p)^a, the lower tail model sharpens; RMT mismatch indicates hidden structure.
first_step: Compute variance of R(p) − M_BM(p) in windows and its scaling with log p for p ≤ 10⁸ (repo data).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Free probability / random multiplicative functions: replace (·/p) by random ±1 multiplicative f
connection: Random multiplicative function models (Harper) ↔ T(p) with Legendre symbol replaced by Steinhaus/Rademacher multiplicative f.
why: Harper's 'better than square-root cancellation' for random multiplicative sums suggests T(p) behaves better than worst case; quantifies M_BM lower bound tightness.
first_step: Simulate T_f = Σ f(u)f(B)·(−1-twist)/φ(4uB) for random multiplicative f and compare distribution to empirical T(p).

title: Entropy/information-theoretic view: bits of p needed to specify a certificate
connection: A certificate (u,B,C) has ~3 log log p bits beyond p ↔ information about p revealed by existence of a certificate.
why: If certificate existence for p were 'hard information', compression arguments (Kolmogorov) could say something; at least clarifies that certificates are tiny relative to p.
first_step: Compute the empirical entropy of the minimal certificate (u,C) distribution conditioned on p mod small moduli; does p mod 840·k predict it?

title: Fokker–Planck / diffusion model of log R(p) along p
connection: log R(p) as a stochastic process in p ↔ smooth main term plus noise.
why: Autocorrelation of R across nearby primes (p, p+840k) shows whether difficulty is local in residue or random.
first_step: Compute autocorrelation of R(p)/M(p) between primes in the same class mod 840 with lag k.

title: Kinetic theory of the 'trial division' process: occupancy problem
connection: Balls-in-bins: each trial modulus m 'catches' p if p ≡ r_m mod m ↔ ES is non-empty-catch.
why: Occupancy problems with heterogeneous bin probabilities have sharp zero-probability estimates (Poisson clumping heuristic, Aldous).
first_step: Apply Aldous' Poisson clumping heuristic to ES with clumps = shared-factor moduli; compute adjusted zero probability.

title: Interactive proofs: verifier checks ES for random p quickly — PCP-style 'ES holds on a dense set' certificates
connection: Probabilistically checkable statements ↔ almost-all ES; verifying 'ES for all p ≤ N' needs a list; can one compress the list into a short certificate (e.g. a few polynomial identities + exceptions)?
why: Compression of the verification certificate is equivalent to finding uniform structure; measuring compressibility (MDL) of the verification list is an experimental structure probe.
first_step: Take the list of minimal certificates for p ≤ 10⁷ and compute how many 'polynomial-family rules' are needed to cover 99%, 99.9%, … (greedy set cover).

title: Subset products in (ℤ/q)^× of random elements: probability −1 is hit with k elements
connection: Random model: k random elements of (ℤ/q)^×, probability some subproduct = −1 ↔ ES slice success probability given Ω(4Cp+1) = k.
why: Exact probabilities (from group structure: needs −1 in generated subgroup and a subproduct, not just subgroup element) give a refined heuristic for R(p) zero probability.
first_step: Compute exactly for q = 4C ≤ 200, k ≤ 6 the probability that subset products of k uniform elements include −1 (with constraint product of all ≡ −1·something?).

title: Hidden constraint: the product of all prime factors of 4Cp+1 is ≡ 1 mod 4C — subproduct ≡ −1 ⟺ complementary subproduct ≡ −1
connection: Since 4Cp+1 ≡ 1 mod 4C, d ≡ −1 ⟺ N/d ≡ −1: symmetric ↔ random-model must condition on total product ≡ 1.
why: Getting the conditioning right changes the predicted zero probability (repo's evenness). Sanity for all random models above.
first_step: Incorporate total-product conditioning into the subset-product model of the previous item and recompute probabilities.

title: Meta: 'one-sided lower tail' theorem hunt across all of mathematics
connection: FRONTIER: needed form is R(p) ≥ εM at every p ↔ search for any theorem of shape 'count ≥ ε·mean for every member' with polylog mean.
why: Repo found none; widening search to combinatorics (e.g. Ramsey-type guaranteed counts, Kővári–Sós–Turán, supersaturation) may produce precedents: supersaturation theorems give pointwise lower tails for counts!
first_step: Look at supersaturation (Erdős–Simonovits): once density exceeds threshold, the number of copies is ≥ c·expected — pointwise in the host structure. Ask whether ES's thick object admits a supersaturation formulation.

title: Random walks on (ℤ/q)^× generated by prime factors: cutoff and mixing of subset products
connection: Subset products of k random elements of an abelian group G cover G once k ≳ log|G| (Erdős–Rényi random subset products). ES wants −1 covered with k ≈ log log p generators: a 'pre-cutoff' regime.
why: Random-walk theory is precise about pre-cutoff probabilities; combined across many levels C it gives a heuristic failure probability.
first_step: Compute P(−1 ∈ subset-products) for k random elements of (ℤ/4C)^× by exact enumeration; plug into a Poisson model over C ≤ C₀.
alt_first_steps: [free_opus-0320] For hard p and C ≤ 50, compute the subproduct distribution's Fourier coefficients and the TV distance from uniform on the generated subgroup.
[tools-0094] Compute the distribution of random subproducts of prime factors of N in (ℤ/e)^× and compare P(−1) with 1/φ(e)·#subproducts.
refs: Erdős–Rényi, Probabilistic methods in group theory (1965)
Diaconis, Group Representations in Probability and Statistics (1988)

title: Probabilistic method with alterations: random p-tied object then fix
connection: Erdős's alteration method ↔ choose random C, get N = 4Cp+1 with random factorisation; ES needs the class gate. Alteration: multiply/divide by small primes to fix the class? (not allowed: N is fixed).
why: Recorded as a check that the alteration freedom ES lacks is precisely 'modifying N'. The I3 form with t free gives N = tp+1 for all t — more freedom.
first_step: Compute success probability per t in I3 slices vs per C in (★); confirm the extra freedom quantitatively.

title: Symmetric-function view: e₂/e₃ = 4/n and the power-sum moments of solutions
connection: For solutions (x,y,z), power sums p_k relate to e_i via Newton ↔ distribution of (x/p, y/p, z/p) shape statistics.
why: Shape statistics (e.g. ratios y/x) of all solutions across p might show a limiting distribution consistent with the main-term density; deviations hint at structure.
first_step: Compute the empirical distribution of (log y/log p, log z/log p) over all solutions for p ≤ 10⁵ and compare with the predicted density from parametrisations.

title: Generating 'ES-like' random problems with tunable expected count to locate the existence threshold empirically
connection: Synthetic problems: replace p by random integers in classes and restrict menu so expected count μ varies ↔ empirical P(no solution) as a function of μ.
why: Gives an empirical law P(0) ≈ f(μ) for ES-shaped problems; plugging μ ≈ M_BM(p) estimates the risk at any p and calibrates the (J)97 zero law independently of siblings.
first_step: For random odd n ≡ 1 mod 24 up to 10⁸, count (★) certificates with u,B ≤ U for varying U (thus varying μ) and fit P(R_U = 0) vs μ.

title: Maier's matrix method for ES: build primes where the Poisson model under-predicts failures
connection: Maier showed the Cramér model fails in short intervals because small-prime biases correlate events. For ES, choose p in progressions modulo products of small primes (p a square mod many ℓ) and measure R(p) relative to M_BM(p).
why: If R(p)/M_BM(p) is systematically smaller on such 'Maier primes', the one-sided H⁻_BM is at risk; if not, it is evidence the BM normalisation already absorbs the Maier effect.
first_step: Take primes p ≡ 1 mod 840·∏ℓ with p a QR mod every ℓ ≤ 50, p ≈ 10¹²; compute R(p)/M_BM(p) vs. random primes of same size.

title: Granville's corrected Cramér model ↔ BM-corrected Poisson model for R(p)
connection: Granville refined Cramér's model by sieving small primes, predicting larger gaps (ξ ≥ 2e^{−γ}). ES's analogue is replacing the naive density 1/(4uC−1) by 1/φ and then by the BM-corrected main term.
why: A precise 'Granville-type' ES model would predict the maximal size of log P(R = 0 | M) and hence whether finitely many failures are expected.
first_step: Fit P(R*(n) = 0 | M_BM(n)) on odd non-squares ≤ 10⁸ against e^{−cM} with c from a sieved Poisson model.
refs: unverified: Granville 1995, Harald Cramér and the distribution of prime numbers (Scand. Actuarial J.)

title: Derandomised Janson: P(no certificate) ≤ exp(−μ + Δ/2) in a pseudorandom model
connection: Janson's inequality bounds the probability that no event occurs among weakly dependent monotone events. For fixed p, with μ = expected certificates ≍ log²p and Δ the pair-dependency sum, a derandomised Janson (pseudorandomness of p's residues) would give R(p) > 0 when μ − Δ/2 → ∞.
why: Connects the campaign's Poisson zero-law heuristics to a precise inequality; the measured zero law (≈ 1.5–2.8 × swap-Poisson) says what Δ must be.
first_step: Compute μ and Δ for the (★) events (indexed by (u,B,C)) at test p, and compare exp(−μ + Δ/2) with the observed zero probability at the same M.
alt_first_steps: [signature-0066] Compute Δ (pair correlation of level events) for hard primes ≤ 10⁸ to see whether μ − Δ grows like log²p.
[tools-0039] Compute μ and Δ empirically for a hard prime; test Riordan–Warnke's 'Janson inequality for general events' conditions.
[translate-0144] Re-read EXSET_ARITH_JANSON_*.md; record the exact place where the fixed-p model needs an unproved independence.
refs: Riordan–Warnke, The Janson inequalities for general up-sets, Random Struct. Alg. 46 (2015)

title: Branching processes for solution-tree growth
connection: Solution-tree problems share F24, F38, F39 and model repeated involutive moves as branching orbits.
why: Tree growth statistics could predict the number of distinct witnesses generated from a seed, while exposing cycles.
first_step: Determine whether the ES transformation graph is locally tree-like at bounded height and calculate its first-return probabilities.

title: Heuristic exceptional-set size for ES and for (★) alone: Σ_n exp(−M(n)) vs. proved bounds
connection: Under the Poisson model with mean M(n) ≍ log²n the expected number of failures ≤ N is Σ exp(−c log²n) < ∞, while for single lines it diverges. Shares F24, F05, F40.
why: Quantifies the 'distance' between the proved exceptional bound (N exp(−c(log N)^{3/4})) and the heuristic truth (O(1)).
first_step: Compute Σ_{n≤N} exp(−M_BM(n)) numerically for N = 10⁸ with the measured zero-law constant; compare with observed (★) failure counts.

title: Smallest-solution size statistics: max denominator of the best ES solution vs. p^θ
connection: ES witnesses have size ≤ poly(p) (F32). The distribution of the minimal possible max-denominator (or minimal level C) over hard primes is an observable comparable to 'least witness' problems (least nonresidue ≪ log² p under GRH, least prime in AP). Note (★) has no level at all for 14 primes ≤ 10¹⁰, so the level statistic needs the union with other lines.
why: If the least witness is always ≤ (log p)^A (in level coordinates) a bounded-search proof shape becomes plausible — B1 says no fixed bound works, but a log-power bound is untouched by B1.
first_step: For hard primes ≤ 10⁹ record the minimal C with R_C(p) > 0 and minimal max(x,y,z)/p; fit against log p.

title: Banks–Ford–Tao: probabilistic prime models fail → refine the ES zero law
connection: BFT (Invent. 2023) show Cramér-type random models of primes mispredict large gaps and propose corrected models; the campaign's (J)97 lottery zero law for ES failures is a random model of the same kind.
why: Siblings fail less than the zero law predicts (G4); a BFT-style correction (sieving by small primes first) could explain it.
first_step: Rebuild the ES lottery model with residue-class sieving by primes ≤ z (BFT 'Granville model') and refit to S_{n,−4} and ES_Q1 failure data.
refs: Banks–Ford–Tao, Large prime gaps and probabilistic models, arXiv:1908.08613

title: Random multiplicative function model of (·/p) on divisor-generated sets (Harper's low moments)
connection: Model (·/p) restricted to S₃(p) by a random multiplicative function f. Then ES₅ failure is 'f ≡ 1 on a structured set'. Harper showed better-than-square-root cancellation for Σ f(n) (low moments), so multiplicative structure reduces fluctuations.
why: It is the native probabilistic model for character values with multiplicative constraints; it gives a heuristic failure probability that respects multiplicative dependencies among elements of S₃(p).
first_step: Compute the multiplicative dependency rank of S₃(p) (dimension of the F₂-span of its exponent vectors over primes). The failure probability under the model is 2^{−rank}; compare with observed.
alt_first_steps: [tools-0036] Model R(p) as Σ_C Σ_{d | 4Cp+1} 1_{d≡−1 (4C)} with prime factorizations randomized, and compute its lower-tail exponent by simulation vs Harper-type predictions.
refs: Harper, Moments of random multiplicative functions, I (Forum Math Pi 2020)
Harper, Moments of random multiplicative functions, I: low moments, better than squareroot cancellation, and critical multiplicative chaos, arXiv:1703.06654

title: Kozma–Samotij lower tails via relative entropy for R(p)
connection: Kozma–Samotij prove lower-tail large deviations for subgraph counts via relative entropy; R(p) is a count of 'arithmetic subgraphs' (divisor relations) in a random-like structure.
why: ES's core difficulty is the one-sided lower tail R(p) ≥ ε·M_BM(p); entropy methods are the modern lower-tail tool.
first_step: Map the ES certificate count to a polynomial in independent-ish Bernoulli variables (ℓ | 4Cp+1) and check the KS hypotheses (bounded influence) on data.
refs: Kozma–Samotij, Lower tails via relative entropy, arXiv:2104.04850

title: Is ES critical or supercritical? Fractional expectation threshold of the level hypergraph
connection: Park–Pham relate thresholds to expectation thresholds. The repo measures ≈ (0.44 → 0.97)·log p expected hit levels (critical regime). Compute, in a random model matching ES's level statistics, the threshold for 'some level hits' and see whether ES sits above it by a growing margin.
why: If ES is only 'critically' above threshold in natural models, any proof must exploit non-random structure; if supercritical, second-moment-type methods are favoured.
first_step: Simulate the matched random model and compute P(no hit) as a function of the scaling parameter; compare with data for hard primes.
alt_first_steps: [tools-0072] Model prime factors of 4Cp+1 (C ≤ X) as independent with Mertens probabilities, compute expectation threshold vs actual threshold numerically.
[upgrades-0142] Compute the fractional expectation threshold of the (★) certificate family for test p using LP over levels.
refs: arXiv:2203.17207 (Park-Pham, A proof of the Kahn-Kalai conjecture)
Park–Pham, A proof of the Kahn–Kalai conjecture, arXiv:2203.17207

title: Frankston–Kahn–Narayanan–Park fractional expectation thresholds / spread measures
connection: FKNP show spread measures on hypergraph edges imply threshold behaviour; ES certificates could be weighted by a spread measure over (C,d) pairs.
why: Constructing a spread measure on ES certificates is a concrete combinatorial goal that would imply a probabilistic 'certificate exists'.
first_step: Define the uniform measure on Type I certificate patterns and compute its spread parameter q on data.
refs: Frankston–Kahn–Narayanan–Park, Thresholds versus fractional expectation-thresholds, Ann. Math. 194 (2021), arXiv:1910.13433

title: Talagrand / Kahn–Kalai expectation thresholds (OAI 175, claimed) for ES monotone events
connection: OAI family 175 claims integral and fractional expectation thresholds agree up to a constant; if ES(p) is modelled as a monotone event over random divisibility indicators, threshold statements tighten.
why: Removes the log factor from Park–Pham-type bounds in a model; calibration of the ES heuristic.
first_step: Read OAI 175 statement and recompute the ES random-model threshold without the log ℓ factor.

title: Keating–Snaith / random-matrix models for families in the ES character expansion
connection: RMT predicts moments of L-function families; ES counts expand over Dirichlet characters mod 4C, i.e. involve families of L-values / character sums.
why: If the ES count's fluctuating part is governed by an L-function family, RMT predicts its distribution, including lower tails.
first_step: Identify the family of L-functions (if any) whose values weight the ES count (via Eisenstein coefficients) and check its symmetry type.
refs: Keating–Snaith, Random matrix theory and ζ(1/2+it), Comm. Math. Phys. 214 (2000)
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Heap–Radziwiłł–Soundararajan sharp fractional moments → lower tails
connection: HRS give sharp upper bounds for fractional moments of ζ; small-moment control is equivalent to lower-tail information for log-normal-like quantities.
why: If log R(p) were approximately Gaussian (log-normal counts), fractional moments of R would control P(R small).
first_step: Fit the distribution of log R(p) at p ≤ 10^8 (data exists) and test log-normality; compute fractional moments.
refs: Heap–Radziwiłł–Soundararajan, Sharp upper bounds for fractional moments of the Riemann zeta function, Q. J. Math. 70 (2019)

title: Fake-ES models: same local statistics, almost-all holds, infinitely many failures
connection: Kahane–Katznelson show a.e. results can be sharp for any null set. Build synthetic 'ES-like' problems (random divisor data with ES's congruence statistics, or ES with a perturbed rule) where Vaughan's proof goes through verbatim but failures are infinite; the real proof must use a feature the fakes lack.
why: Identifies which properties of the integers any ES proof must use — the constructive face of the barrier map.
first_step: Construct a random model of 'divisors of 4Cp+1' with independent prime-factor classes, run the almost-all argument, and check what pointwise statement fails.
alt_first_steps: [tools-0219] Build a model: random integers with correct local divisibility but with an added sparse 'conspiracy' making all certificates fail for p in a thin set; check consistency with ET averages and Vaughan.
refs: Kolmogorov, Fund. Math. 4 (1923)/ C. R. 1926 (everywhere divergent L^1 Fourier series)

title: Statistical change-point tests on hardness vs p (detecting new obstruction scales)
connection: Change-point and extreme-value statistics detect regime shifts; ES min-count/log²p over p ≤ 10^8 and adversarial data at 10^25 could reveal a scale where hardness behaves differently.
why: A detected trend in normalised minimum would inform P(ES false) calibrations.
first_step: Fit an extreme-value (Gumbel/GEV) model to block minima of f(p)/log²p over dyadic ranges and extrapolate the expected minimum at 10^30.
refs: Coles, An Introduction to Statistical Modeling of Extreme Values (2001)

title: OAI 011 Poisson–Dirichlet law for prime factors of p−1 → law for factors of p+e
connection: OAI 011 claims the ordered normalised log prime factors of p−1 converge to PD(1); the e-slice integers (p+e)/4 are shifted primes for fixed e.
why: A PD(1) law for shifted primes p+e (fixed e) gives the distribution of the 'generator set' of the ES quotient set across p — the right random model for e-slice success.
first_step: Compute the empirical law of prime-factor log-ratios of (p+3)/4 for p ≤ 10^8 and compare with PD(1); then simulate e-slice success under PD(1).

title: OAI 006 Goldfeld densities (claimed) — rank-parity as a model for ES parity layers
connection: OAI 006 claims Goldfeld's conjecture for quadratic twists; ES's parity layers (R(p)/2 mod 2 fair coin) resemble root-number parity statistics in twist families.
why: Root numbers are local products — a fully local parity; ES parity looks random — comparing clarifies whether an ES 'root number' exists.
first_step: Test whether R(p)/2 mod 2 is predicted by any product of local symbols (p/ℓ) for small ℓ via logistic regression.

title: Kubilius model / PD anatomy for the p-tied integer 4Cp+1
connection: The Kubilius model replaces ω-type statistics of integers by independent prime indicators; Granville's anatomy shows prime factors follow PD(1).
why: A precise anatomy model of 4Cp+1 (C varying, p fixed) predicts the full distribution of R(p), including the lower tail.
first_step: Simulate R(p) under a Kubilius/PD model with the exact local factors at small primes and compare its lower tail with data at p ≤ 10^8.
refs: Granville, Anatomy of integers and permutations (2008 lecture notes)

title: Gaussian multiplicative chaos limit for divisor-class counting functions
connection: Critical GMC describes limits of random multiplicative functions' partial sums and of |ζ| on short intervals (Saksman–Webb); the ES count is a divisor-sum over a random-like factorisation.
why: GMC is the established mechanism behind non-Gaussian lower tails of such sums.
first_step: Compute the random-model R(p) distribution and check for GMC-type log-correlated structure (variance ~ log log).
refs: Saksman–Webb, The Riemann zeta function and Gaussian multiplicative chaos: statistics on the critical line, Ann. Prob. 48 (2020)

title: Barban–Davenport–Halberstam variance for ES counts in APs of p
connection: BDH gives the variance of prime counts over all residue classes; an analogous variance for ES counts f(p) across p mod q would quantify residue-class structure of hardness.
why: The repo's 'failure profile carries nothing beyond p mod M' claim is a variance statement in disguise.
first_step: Compute Σ_{a mod q} (Σ_{p≡a, p≤x} f(p) − expected)² for q ≤ 1000 and compare with a BDH-type prediction.
refs: Montgomery, Primes in arithmetic progressions, Michigan Math. J. 17 (1970)

title: Selberg–Delange for class-restricted divisor generating functions
connection: Selberg–Delange gives asymptotics for Σ a(n) when Σ a(n)n^{−s} ≈ ζ(s)^z G(s); the indicator 'N has no divisor ≡ −1 (mod m)' has Dirichlet series with a fractional zeta power (prime factors in a subgroup).
why: Exact asymptotics for counts of N with no class-divisor give the baseline failure probability per slice.
first_step: Compute the Selberg–Delange exponent z for 'all prime factors in a subgroup H ∌ −1 of (ℤ/m)^×' and the resulting density x(log x)^{z−1}.
refs: Tenenbaum, Introduction to Analytic and Probabilistic Number Theory (3rd ed. 2015), II.5

title: Inverse Littlewood–Offord (Tao–Vu, Nguyen–Vu) for signed subset products hitting −1
connection: For squarefree N = ∏ℓ_i, the e-slice quotient ab⁻¹ (ab | N) is ∏ ℓ_i^{ε_i} with ε_i ∈ {−1,0,1} — a signed 'Littlewood–Offord walk' in (ℤ/e)^×. Inverse LO theorems say a walk concentrates on one value only if the steps are structured (lie in a small GAP/subgroup).
why: Gives the right language for ES's e-slice: the hitting probability of −1 vs the generic 1/|group|, and what structure is needed for systematic failure.
first_step: For hard primes compute, per slice, the distribution of ∏ℓ_i^{ε_i} over all 3^ω sign patterns and compare P(−1) with 1/φ(e); identify slices where steps lie in an index-2 subgroup.
refs: Tao–Vu, Inverse Littlewood–Offord theorems and the condition number of random discrete matrices, Ann. Math. 169 (2009)
Nguyen–Vu, Optimal inverse Littlewood–Offord theorems, Adv. Math. 226 (2011)
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Gowers' quasirandom groups: ABC = SL₂(𝔽_q) for dense A,B,C — local covering for ES₅ words
connection: Gowers (and Nikolov–Pyber) show that if |A||B||C| > |G|³/m (m = minimal nontrivial representation dimension) then ABC = G; ES₅ certificates are length-3 products of letters from fixed sets.
why: Gives a clean local (mod q) surjectivity criterion for length-3 words — the local layer of ES₅ — and quantifies how dense the letter sets must be mod q.
first_step: Compute the reductions mod q of the ES₅ letter sets A, B, C (with entries bounded by p-dependent ranges) and check the Gowers inequality for q ≤ 50.
refs: Gowers, Quasirandom groups, Combin. Probab. Comput. 17 (2008)
Nikolov–Pyber, Product decompositions of quasirandom groups and a Jordan type theorem, JEMS 13 (2011)

title: Shearer / entropy inequalities for joint divisibility of slices
connection: Shearer's lemma bounds joint entropy by marginals; the joint divisibility profile of slices (N_e mod small primes for e in a window) is a random vector whose entropy controls how many 'independent chances' ES gets.
why: Quantifies effective number of independent slices at a fixed p.
first_step: Compute empirical entropies of divisibility profiles across windows of slices at hard vs typical primes.
refs: Chung–Graham–Frankl–Shearer, Some intersection theorems for ordered sets and graphs, JCTA 43 (1986)

title: Chen–Stein Poisson approximation for I3 counts at fixed n
connection: I3 counts at fixed n over t, u, v are sums of weakly dependent divisor events; Poisson approximation predicts P(count = 0).
why: I3 is verified to 10^9 with a known largest exception 2 433 600 — calibrates Poisson-model predictions of the largest exception.
first_step: Fit the Poisson model on n ≤ 10^8 and predict the largest exception; compare with 2 433 600.

title: Kahn–Kalai / Park–Pham on the I3 random model (small groups, many events)
connection: I3's events per n are many (t ranges) with small moduli; threshold theory could predict exactly when 'expected ≥ 1' implies 'present w.h.p.'.
why: I3 is proved-false-free beyond 2 433 600 in data; matching threshold predictions is a sanity test of the method before ES.
first_step: Compute expectation thresholds for I3 events at n ~ 10^6–10^9 in the random model.

title: Large deviations / lower-tail of the certificate count: Poisson vs Gaussian regime
connection: The certificate count N(p) has mean ≍ log²p. P(N(p) = 0) is a lower-tail large deviation. In random-graph theory (Janson–Łuczak–Ruciński) lower tails are governed by Janson's inequality and are exponential in the mean.
why: The lower-tail exponent ≈ mean gives P(0) ≈ p^{−c log p}, summable over p: ES true heuristically. Native LDP theory would quantify the needed dependence structure.
first_step: Fit log P(N = 0 | mean M) from data (repo has it) against the Janson prediction −M/(1+Δ/M); record Δ.

title: Branching-process / tree-search model of the certificate search (Galton–Watson survival)
connection: Searching levels C = 1,2,… and divisor splits gives a search tree; the probability of finding no certificate is an extinction probability of a branching process with offspring ~ divisor counts.
why: Branching processes give exact extinction-probability equations, which give a sharper heuristic than Poisson when certificates cluster.
first_step: Model the per-level offspring distribution from data; solve the extinction equation and compare with observed zero frequencies for ES₅.

title: Large-q limit (Katz–Sarnak) of the ES_q certificate count distribution
connection: As q → ∞ with deg P fixed, counts of certificates become equidistributed statistics governed by monodromy groups (Katz's equidistribution). The probability of zero certificates in the limit is computable.
why: It gives an exact 'random model' limit of the ES count distribution, a rigorous analogue of the Poisson heuristic, and possibly a proof of ES_q for q large relative to the degree.
first_step: Identify the monodromy group of the certificate-counting sheaf (divisor-in-class conditions) and compute the limiting P(count = 0) for small degrees.
refs: Katz–Sarnak, Random Matrices, Frobenius Eigenvalues, and Monodromy (1999)
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Commute time / escape probability on the fan: A/p as a random-walk quantity
connection: For the fan graph, R_eff(a,s) = A/p, so the commute time between a and the sink is 2|E|·A/p and the escape probability from a is 1/(v·R_eff) = p/(vA). The ES sign is a residuosity property of a commute time numerator.
why: Random-walk interpretations allow coupling/monotonicity arguments (Rayleigh monotonicity: adding edges decreases resistance), which could organise words by a partial order.
first_step: Use Rayleigh monotonicity to order words of p by resistance; check whether the sign changes monotonically along chains (data p < 10⁵).
refs: Doyle–Snell, Random Walks and Electric Networks (1984)

title: Borel–Cantelli heuristic: Σ_p P(no certificate at p) < ∞ under various independence models
connection: With P(fail at p) ≈ exp(−c log²p) the sum converges, so heuristically only finitely many failures exist and they would be small (all excluded below 10¹⁸). This is the probabilistic native statement of 'ES is true'.
why: Calibration: makes precise which correlation model must hold for the heuristic, and how much heavier the lower tail would have to be to allow infinitely many failures (log P(0) ≥ −log p).
first_step: From repo LDP data, fit log P(0|M) and compute the threshold tail behaviour that would make Σ_p diverge; compare with Markoff (Ghosh–Sarnak) where infinitely many failures occur.

title: Parametrise ES methods by L(1,(·/p)): one should improve as it grows, another as it shrinks
connection: Holowinsky's bound is in terms of Σ_ℓ (|λ(ℓ)| − 1)/ℓ, Soundararajan's in the opposite tendency. M_BM = M₀ − T(p) is hurt when the weighted sum of (−m/p) is large. Find a second certificate family whose expected count increases with T(p).
why: If the two main terms move in opposite directions with the same character statistic, their sum is bounded below uniformly — Holowinsky–Soundararajan in miniature.
first_step: Compute the expected counts of the b=1 line, windows and ES₅ as functions of the Legendre profile (m/p)_{m ≤ 100}; regress against T(p).
refs: arXiv:0809.1636 (Holowinsky-Soundararajan, Mass equidistribution for Hecke eigenforms)

title: Quasirandom 'one more factor' trick — size check for ES in SL₂(F_p)
connection: Nikolov–Pyber: if |A||B||C| > |G|³/m then ABC = G. For ES words A·T·A in SL₂(F_p), |A| ≈ |T| ≈ p while |G|³/m ≈ p⁸: the trick fails by a huge margin; quantify the deficit and check whether replacing SL₂(F_p) by a smaller quotient (Borel, affine group) helps.
why: Records why the canonical almost→every group trick does not apply directly, and where a smaller ambient group might restore it.
first_step: Compute |A|, |T|, |G| and m for G = SL₂(F_p), the Borel subgroup and the affine group F_p ⋊ F_p*; find the smallest ambient group in which ES becomes a product-covering statement.

title: Keevash template: algebraic identity families + random perturbation for square classes
connection: Keevash's randomized algebraic construction starts from an algebraic template and perturbs it. ES: Mordell identities cover all non-square classes mod 840 (algebraic template); perturb identity parameters randomly to handle the square classes, with an absorber for failures.
why: Mordell–Schinzel forbids polynomial identities covering squares, but random perturbations of identities are not identities.
first_step: Take Mordell's identities, introduce free integer parameters (k-fold families), and measure how often random parameter choices give certificates for primes in square classes.

title: Entropy inequality for the union of certificate families
connection: Gilmer's entropy argument shows some element is frequent in a union-closed family. ES certificate families are 'union-like' (if a family works for p it works for multiples); an entropy inequality on the joint distribution of certificate indicators across families might force a frequently-successful family.
why: Odd, but entropy methods recently produced constant-factor every-family results from nothing.
first_step: Compute the empirical joint distribution of success indicators of 10 certificate families over primes ≤ 10⁷ and the entropy of their union.
refs: arXiv:2211.09055 (Gilmer, A constant lower bound for the union-closed sets conjecture)

title: Entropic Ruzsa distance between divisor-class distributions at different levels
connection: GGMT proved PFR via entropic Ruzsa distance and an entropy-decrement iteration. For fixed p, the distributions of divisor classes of 4Cp+1 across levels C could be compared via entropic distances; structured failure would force small distances to subgroup-uniform distributions.
why: An odd but well-defined way to quantify 'subgroup trapping' of divisor classes across levels.
first_step: Compute entropic distances of the divisor-class distributions to uniform-on-subgroup distributions for hard p.
refs: arXiv:2311.05762 (Gowers-Green-Manners-Tao, On a conjecture of Marton)

title: Left-tail extrapolation: does Σ_p P(R(p) = 0) converge?
connection: Goldbach's other conjecture failed at 5777/5993 where the expected representation count was small. For ES, extrapolate the measured zero law (P(R* = 0 | M)) to estimate Σ_p P(no certificate) over p > 10¹⁸; if it is ≪ 10⁻⁶, the 'heuristic' evidence for ES is overwhelming, and the computation identifies which sub-route is safest to target.
why: Sanity-checks which formulations are heuristically true for all p (needed before trying to prove them).
first_step: Fit log P(R* = 0 | M) on the repo's data and integrate against the distribution of M(p) for p > 10¹⁸; do the same for (★), b=1, union.

title: AKS-style 'too large and too small' group argument for a counterexample
connection: AKS: if n is not a prime power, a group of polynomials would be both ≥ a binomial lower bound and ≤ n^{√t}. ES: if p has no certificate, the set of divisor classes of 4Cp+1 across levels generates a structure (e.g. a subgroup of Π_C (ℤ/4C)* avoiding all −1's) that might be shown both large (many independent prime factors across C) and small (avoidance).
why: The most striking conditional→unconditional derandomisation used exactly this double counting.
first_step: Define G_K(p) = subgroup of Π_{C≤K} (ℤ/4C)* generated by the vectors (q mod 4C)_C over primes q > 4K dividing some 4Cp+1 (so q is a unit at every level); compute its index and whether it avoids the −1 pattern for hard p.

title: Entropy count of near-certificates vs defect buckets
connection: Spencer's partial colouring needs (#objects) > (#buckets)·(something). For ES, near-certificates of p with defect δ in a set of size Q number ~ p^{a}; buckets (defect, residues) number ~ Q^{b}. If a > b·log Q / log p, collisions are forced; compute a and b for concrete combination laws.
why: A pure counting check that tells whether any pigeonhole + combination mechanism can possibly work for ES.
first_step: For the SL₂-form near-certificates (det = 1 + δ with |δ| ≤ Δ), count objects with entries ≤ p and the number of congruence buckets needed for the quotient to be integral.
refs: Spencer, Trans. AMS 289 (1985) 679-706 (Six standard deviations suffice)

title: 4/n as a sum of three reciprocals of squares (Graham-type world)
connection: Graham characterized rationals that are finite sums of reciprocals of distinct squares. The 3-term version 4/n = 1/a² + 1/b² + 1/c² is a sparse world with local obstructions.
why: Not equivalent to ES, but a sibling in which local/global behaviour can be determined fully; it tests whether square-type obstructions come back with square denominators.
first_step: Compute for n ≤ 10^5 which n admit 4/n = Σ 1/a_i² (3 terms) and look for congruence patterns.
alt_first_steps: [signature-0444] Check whether 'a/n = 1/x² + 1/y² + 1/z²' has a known local-global theory; record its obstruction set for small numerators.
refs: R. L. Graham, On finite sums of reciprocals of distinct nth powers, Pacific J. Math. 14 (1964) 85–92

title: Mixed: 4/n = 1/x + 1/y + 1/z² (one square denominator)
connection: One square denominator keeps the problem 2-dimensional but couples to quadratic residues. It is a sibling where the T1 square obstruction might be amplified or cancelled.
why: If it is always solvable via an identity involving z² ≡ something, it gives a new certificate type over Z.
first_step: Brute force n ≤ 10^4; for each solvable n record the class of z mod small primes.

title: Breusch/Stewart: every rational with odd denominator is a finite sum of distinct odd unit fractions
connection: Solved universal unit-fraction statement under a parity restriction; ES fixed-length with no parity constraint. Note: for odd n, 4/n with all three denominators odd is impossible (4xyz is even but n(xy+yz+zx) is odd), so ES at odd n always uses an even denominator.
why: Parity restrictions change term counts dramatically — a clean feature-flip for the 2-adic side of ES (F29).
first_step: Compute: for primes p ≤ 10⁶, does 4/p always have a 3-term solution with all denominators odd? (Certainly not when … check quickly.)
alt_first_steps: [signature-0078] Determine the possible 2-adic valuation patterns (v₂(x), v₂(y), v₂(z)) of ES solutions at hard primes ≤ 10⁵.

title: Landau's class equation and fusion-category Egyptian equations: 1 = Σ 1/|C(g_i)|
connection: Integral modular categories and finite groups yield Egyptian equations for 1 (Landau; Bruillard–Rowell). A group with 4 conjugacy classes gives 1 − 1/|G| = three unit fractions, an ES-type equation with numerator |G| − 1.
why: Shows ES-like equations arising from algebraic structures where existence is guaranteed by constructions; the analogous numerator family (N−1)/N is a sibling world.
first_step: Enumerate (N−1)/N = 1/a + 1/b + 1/c solutions and compare with groups having 4 classes (Z₄, V₄, D₅, A₄); note which equations are 'realized'.

title: Algebraic combinatorics: q-analogue of ES (q-integers [n]_q) and its solvability
connection: Replace n by [n]_q = 1 + q + … + q^{n−1}: 4/[n]_q = Σ 1/[x_i]_q in ℚ(q)? ↔ q-deformations sometimes make problems rigid.
why: If a q-analogue has polynomial-identity solutions, specialising q → 1 might give ES; Mordell–Schinzel suggests obstruction persists, but the q-world has extra freedom (cyclotomic factorisations of [n]_q).
first_step: Search x, y, z ≤ 60, n ≤ 60 for exact identities in Q(q) using polynomial arithmetic.
alt_first_steps: [free_opus-0326] Search for solutions of 4/[p]_q = 1/A(q) + 1/B(q) + 1/C(q) with A,B,C ∈ ℤ[q] for small primes p via polynomial factorisation of [p]_q-related expressions.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: xy + yz + zx = N (Borwein–Choi): a symmetric ternary problem solved up to one possible exception (none under GRH)
connection: Borwein–Choi determine the N not of the form xy + yz + zx (x, y, z ≥ 1) — 18 known exceptions plus at most one more unconditionally, the extra one excluded under GRH — via class numbers of Q(√−N). For an ES solution, xy + yz + zx = 4xyz/n (the pretzel determinant).
why: The same symmetric quadratic in x, y, z appears in ES; their class-number method (representations ↔ forms of discriminant −4N) is a proved-twin technique for a closely related equation.
first_step: Read Borwein–Choi (Exp. Math. 9 (2000)) and identify how r_{σ₂}(n) is written as a class-number sum; look for an analogous expression of the ES count on the slice σ₂ = 4σ₃/n.

refs: Borwein–Choi, 'On the representations of xy+yz+zx', Experiment. Math. 9 (2000)

title: Ternary Goldbach (proved) vs binary Goldbach (open): where ES sits
connection: Ternary problems with power-size expected counts are proved by the circle method; binary ones are open. ES at fixed p has expected count ≍ log²p, smaller than binary Goldbach's ≍ p/log²p — ES is 'sub-binary', so circle-method-type methods are not expected to work pointwise.
why: Calibrates expectations: pointwise ES needs structure (algebraic identities, reciprocity) rather than analysis; analytic methods only give almost-all.
first_step: Context; record the comparison of expected counts in the memo header.

title: Agoh–Giuga and Egyptian divisibility: Σ 1/p_i − 1/Π p_i ∈ ℤ
connection: Giuga numbers satisfy Σ_{p|n} 1/p − 1/n ∈ ℤ. Egyptian equations over prime denominators with a correction term are another sibling with open status (Agoh–Giuga conjecture).
why: Prime-denominator Egyptian equations are very rigid; a technique for Giuga-type equations might apply to ES with prime-power denominators.

title: Lehmer's totient problem: Egyptian-type constraints ∏(1 − 1/p) from φ(n) | n − 1
connection: φ(n) | n − 1 implies inequalities and Egyptian-type relations on the prime factors. Another rigid multiplicative/Egyptian sibling with open status.
why: Methods to bound or exclude solutions there might adapt to proving rigidity (non-existence) in constrained ES worlds, i.e. explaining their failure sets.
first_step: Low priority.

title: Primitive prime divisors (Zsigmondy/Bang) as the integer replacement for 'units' in proved worlds
connection: In Z[1/ℓ] the universal divisor comes from 1 + ℓ^k; Zsigmondy guarantees new prime factors of a^k ± 1. Over Z the corresponding p-tied integers (4Cp + 1) have no such algebraic factor structure.
why: If p-tied integers with Zsigmondy-like algebraic factorizations exist (e.g. p^k + 1 or 4p^k + 1 families), they supply 'universal divisors' p-dependently — power-ladder certificates.
first_step: List ES certificate families involving p^k ± 1 or similar (power ladders); check POWER_LADDER_ES.md for the state of the art.

title: Prime-denominator world (Luca–Pappalardi title world): 4/p with all denominators in {p, primes, 2·primes}
connection: Denominators restricted to primes or twice primes is a very sparse world; 'x prime' alone fails at 260/499 below 8000. Full prime-type restriction probably fails almost always.
why: Gives a lower anchor for lottery calibration (very few tickets → mostly failures).
first_step: Compute for p < 8000 the 'all denominators in {primes, 2·primes, p·small}' world.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Word-map monodromy (finite flat covers t,u,v ↦ tuv − u − v) has no integer analogue — find one?
connection: EXSET_FUNCTION_FIELD 7′ uses monodromy groups of word covers (CFSG ⇒ Alt) to bound large-q exceptional densities by exp(−Ω(n²)). Over Z, the analogue would be a 'Galois group' for the factorization of n + v as tuv − u − v… — no known integer analogue.
why: Integer 'monodromy' could be modelled by Chebotarev in the splitting fields of the polynomial family X·Y·Z − Y − Z − n over Q(n) (Hilbert irreducibility); its Galois group controls the density of n with a word of a given shape.
first_step: Compute the Galois group over Q(n) of the polynomial system defining words of a fixed shape and compare with the FF G_{n,p}.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: ES over F_q with a cone = an index-2 subgroup (squares): the 'quadratic positivity' finite world
connection: In F_q, require x, y, z to be non-zero squares. Solvability of 4/n = Σ 1/x_i with squares is a question about the diagonal quadric Σ a_i w_i^{−2}… — solvable for q large by Weil; failures only for small q.
why: Small-q failures of 'quadratic positivity' indicate how much a sign-type restriction can obstruct in a finite world — a calibration of T1-like effects at the level of a single prime.
first_step: Brute force for q ≤ 50: for which q and n does 4/n = Σ 1/x_i with x_i nonzero squares have no solution?
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: FF analogue of hard-prime structure: P with P − 1 'smooth' (many small-degree factors)
connection: Over Z, constrained-world failures cluster at p with smooth p − 1 (601, 1801, 2521). In F_q[T] the analogue is P with P − 1 (or P + c) having many small factors; FF exceptional P's can be checked for this property.
why: If the same 'smooth shift ⇒ hard' pattern appears in FF where proofs exist, the FF proofs explain how such P are still covered — a template for Z.
first_step: From FF exception lists (EXSET_FUNCTION_FIELD data), compute the factorization degree profile of P − 1 for failing vs non-failing P.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Catalog: n = p + 2^a + 2^b (Crocker)
connection: n = p + 2^a + 2^b (Crocker) ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: ≍ log n. Obstruction: no single-modulus covering; failures come from an explicit sparse family. Status: false infinitely often (Crocker 1971; Pan 2011 gives ≫ x^{1−ε} odd exceptions ≤ x). Mechanism: an explicit sparse family of odd n (check whether it is built from 2^{2^m}−1 and Fermat-number divisibility, as commonly described).
why: Log-count, no covering, still false i.o. — the sharpest warning that 'log² count + no local obstruction' is not enough; ES's count is log² p.
first_step: Read Crocker 1971 (Pacific J. Math.) and isolate the exact structural input; ask whether an ES analogue (p tied to 2^{2^m}) exists among primes.

title: Catalog: odd n = p + 2^a + 2^b + 2^c (Sun's conjecture: every odd n > 8)
connection: odd n = p + 2^a + 2^b + 2^c (Sun's conjecture: every odd n > 8) ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: ≍ log² n — same order as ES. Obstruction: none known. Status: open (conjectured by Z.-W. Sun, arXiv:0901.3075). Mechanism: none; numerics only.
why: Exact twin of ES in expected count (log²) with additive instead of multiplicative witnesses; any proof or disproof calibrates ES directly.
first_step: Check whether Crocker's construction extends to three powers (search 'p+2^a+2^b+2^c exceptions'); compute min witness count / log² n up to 10^9.

title: Catalog: Riesel numbers k·2^n − 1 (509203)
connection: Riesel numbers k·2^n − 1 (509203) ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: divergent log, periodic parameter. Obstruction: covering. Status: false for specific k; minimality open. Mechanism: covering.

title: Catalog: Brier numbers (both Sierpiński and Riesel)
connection: Brier numbers (both Sierpiński and Riesel) ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: divergent log. Obstruction: simultaneous coverings. Status: exist (explicit large k). Mechanism: two coverings.
why: Simultaneous covering of two linear families is possible — relevant if ES were reduced to two simultaneous divisor conditions.

title: Catalog: n − 2^k composite for all k (Erdős; e.g. via covering)
connection: n − 2^k composite for all k (Erdős; e.g. via covering) ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: O(1). Obstruction: covering. Status: infinitely many such odd n. Mechanism: covering.

title: Catalog: n = p + F_k (prime + Fibonacci number)
connection: n = p + F_k (prime + Fibonacci number) ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: O(1). Obstruction: covering congruences on the Fibonacci orbit (periodic mod m, Pisano period). Status: check whether: positive proportion represented and an AP of failures known (Wu–Sun style). Mechanism: Pisano periodicity makes covering possible.

title: Catalog: Romanoff density for p + 2^k (lower density)

Status: positive lower density proved; upper density < 1/2 (van der Corput / Erdős). Mechanism: Cauchy–Schwarz + sieve upper bound for r(n) second moment.

title: Goldbach's other conjecture and explicit finite exceptions
connection: OEIS A060003 records odd composites not expressible as a prime plus twice a square, with 5777 and 5993 identified as the known exceptions. It shares F01/F03/F25/F32: a universal arithmetic representation, finite explicit failures, and compact certificates checked by divisor/prime search.
